Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH.
These symptoms include a weak urine stream.
They include trouble starting to urinate.
They include dribbling.
They include a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely.
They include needing to urinate often or urgently.
They include getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers.
It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck.
Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there.
This improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day.
Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax.
Flomax has now been discontinued in the U.S.
Generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure.
It is not approved for use in women or children.

Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood.
These medicines can increase the risk of side effects.
The medicines block these enzymes.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
cimetidine
warfarin
medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra).
Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg.
Your doctor will decide what is right for you.

It is used to treat type 1 and type 2 diabetes in certain patients.
The treatment aims to improve and maintain blood glucose levels.
Insulin glargine is a man-made form of human insulin.
It is used once daily.
It provides a base level of insulin.
This insulin keeps working for 24 hours or longer.
Insulin glargine is available under the brand names Lantus, Basaglar, Toujeo, Semglee, and Rezvoglar.
Langlara is an interchangeable biosimilar to Lantus that was FDA-approved on May 4, 2026.

They are approved for use in adult and pediatric patients.
These patients have type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
Basasglar is FDA-approved to be used by adults for type 2 diabetes.
It is also approved for adults and pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes.
In patients with type 1 diabetes, insulin glargine must be used together with a short-acting insulin.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you don't understand how to use an injection.
Prepare an injection only when you are ready to give it.
Do not use it if the medicine looks cloudy, has changed colors, or has particles in it.
Insulin glargine is injected under the skin, using a syringe or insulin pen, once per day at the same time of day.
Insulin can be injected into your upper legs (thighs), upper arms, or stomach area (abdomen).
Do not inject into the same place two times in a row.
Avoid injecting into skin that is damaged, tender, bruised, pitted, thickened, scaly, or has a scar or hard lump.
When treating type 1 diabetes, use your short-acting insulin before meals as directed by your doctor.
Insulin glargine must not be given with an insulin pump or mixed with other insulins.
Do not inject insulin glargine into a vein or a muscle.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of this medicine.

Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Take empagliflozin once a day in the morning, with or without food.
Your blood sugar will need to be checked often.
You may also need to test the level of ketones in your urine.
Empagliflozin can cause life-threatening ketoacidosis (too much acid in the blood).
Contact your doctor if a urine test shows that you have high ketones in the urine.
Even if your blood sugar is normal.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky.
To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda.
Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injection in case of severe hypoglycemia.
You may get dehydrated during prolonged illness.
Call your doctor if you are sick with vomiting or diarrhea.

Empagliflozin may cause serious side effects.

a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out;
low blood sugar -- headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery;

the Furoscix ReadyFlow, a prefilled autoinjector that delivers 80 mg of furosemide in about 10 seconds.

Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke.
This risk is especially high if you use it long term.
The risk is also higher if you take high doses.
The risk is further increased if you have heart disease.
Even people without heart disease or risk factors could have a stroke or heart attack while taking this medicine.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking meloxicam after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to.
You may have an increased risk of another heart attack if you take this medicine after a recent heart attack.
Get emergency medical help if you have chest pain, weakness, shortness of breath, slurred speech, or problems with vision or balance.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding.
This bleeding can be fatal.
These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Call your doctor at once if you have symptoms of stomach bleeding.
These symptoms include black, bloody, or tarry stools.

Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke.
This risk is especially high if you use it long term.
The risk is also higher if you take high doses.
The risk is further increased if you have heart disease.
Even people without heart disease or risk factors could have a stroke or heart attack while taking this medicine.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking meloxicam after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to.
You may have an increased risk of another heart attack if you take this medicine after a recent heart attack.
Get emergency medical help if you have chest pain, weakness, shortness of breath, slurred speech, or problems with vision or balance.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding.
This bleeding can be fatal.
These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Call your doctor at once if you have symptoms of stomach bleeding.
These symptoms include black, bloody, or tarry stools.

candidate_edges.subject: meloxicam
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the adverse effect or symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
liver problems - nausea, upper stomach pain, itching, tired feeling, flu-like symptoms, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay-colored stools, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes);

kidney problems - little or no urination, swelling in your feet or ankles, feeling tired or short of breath.
Common meloxicam side effects may include:
stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, heartburn
diarrhea, constipation, gas;
dizziness; or
cold symptoms, flu symptoms.

Maximum dose: 8 tablets/24 hours

Initial dose: 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
Maximum dose: 6 tablets/24 hours

Initial dose: 15 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
Maximum dose: 90 mL/24 hours

Initial dose: 11.25 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
Maximum dose: 67.5 mL/24 hours
Comments:
Doses should be individually titrated.
The titration should provide adequate analgesia.
The titration should minimize adverse reactions.
The lowest effective dose should be used.
The dose should be used for the shortest duration.
The duration should be consistent with individual patient treatment goals.

Pancreas or gallbladder problems

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common Side Effects:
The possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen are constipation, nausea, sleepiness, vomiting, tiredness, headache, dizziness, and abdominal pain.
Call your healthcare provider if you have any of these symptoms and they are severe.
Get emergency medical help if you have:
Trouble breathing
Shortness of breath
Fast heartbeat
Chest pain
Swelling of your face, tongue, or throat
Extreme drowsiness
Light-headedness when changing positions
Feeling faint
Agitation
High body temperature
Trouble walking
Stiff muscles
Mental changes such as confusion.
These are not all the possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Do not take hydrocodone and acetaminophen if you have:
Severe asthma, trouble breathing, or other lung problems
A bowel blockage or a narrowing of the stomach or intestines
Signs of an allergy, such as a rash
Are allergic to any of its ingredients.
Before taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, tell your healthcare provider if you have a history of:
Head injury, seizures
Liver, kidney, thyroid problems
Problems urinating
Pancreas or gallbladder problems
Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are:
Pregnant or planning to become pregnant.
Prolonged use of hydrocodone and acetaminophen during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby.
These symptoms could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated.
Breastfeeding.
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen pass into breast milk and may harm your baby.
Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness.
Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
candidate_edges.object: other pain treatments do not treat your pain well enough
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be used for the medical purpose or indication specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a strong prescription combination pain medicine.
The medicine contains an opioid, hydrocodone.
The medicine also contains acetaminophen.
Acetaminophen is used to manage moderate to moderately severe pain.
This medicine is used when other pain treatments do not treat your pain well enough.
It is also used when you cannot tolerate other pain treatments.
Other pain treatments include non-opioid pain medicines.
An opioid pain medicine that can put you at risk for overdose and death.
You are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death.
This risk exists even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed.
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a Schedule II controlled substance.
All branded hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco, Vicodin, Lortab, Hycet, Lorcet, Verdrocet, Xodol, Zamicet) have been discontinued.
Generic hydrocodone and acetaminophen tablets and oral solution is still available.
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen first gained FDA approval on May 3, 1982.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
In the Mounjaro prescribing information, SURPASS-1 (NCT03954834) was a 40-week trial.
The trial was in adults with type 2 diabetes.
The adults had blood sugar that was not adequately controlled with diet and exercise alone.
Patients received once-weekly Mounjaro 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg, or placebo.
After 40 weeks, 78% to 85% of adults taking Mounjaro achieved an HbA1c below 7%.
This is compared with 23% of adults taking a placebo.
The average HbA1c change was -1.8% with Mounjaro 5 mg.
The average HbA1c change was -1.7% with Mounjaro 10 mg.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
SURPASS-CVOT randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.
The adults were randomized to Mounjaro (tirzepatide, up to 15 mg once weekly) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly.
Dulaglutide is a GLP-1 medicine already approved to reduce cardiovascular risk.
The study had a median follow-up of about 4 years.
Cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke occurred in 12.1% of those taking Mounjaro.
These events occurred in 13.0% of those taking dulaglutide.
The hazard ratio was 0.92 with a 95% CI of 0.83–1.01.
The results met the trial's goal of non-inferiority.
The results did not demonstrate superiority.
Death from any cause occurred in 8.5% of the Mounjaro group.
Death from any cause occurred in 10.1% of the dulaglutide group.
The hazard ratio was 0.84 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.75–0.94.
This outcome was not a primary endpoint.
This outcome was not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
Therefore, the result should be read as exploratory.
These results describe how Mounjaro performs against another GLP-1.

Vomiting
Constipation
Nausea (mild to moderate)
Decreased appetite
Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:
Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away.
This applies if the pain occurs with or without vomiting.
This also applies if the pain spreads to your back.
Severe stomach pain is a sign of pancreatitis.
Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration.
Dehydration may lead to kidney problems.
Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk.
Tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
Gallbladder problems include severe upper stomach pain.
They include fever.
They include nausea.
They include vomiting.
They include yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice).
They include clay-colored stools.
Serious allergic reactions require seeking emergency medical attention.

Dose of Mounjaro to Reduce Cardiovascular Risk (Adults With Type 2 Diabetes at High Risk):
The same dosing and escalation schedule applies.
Start at 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Increase in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
Continue up to a maximum of 15 mg once a week.
In the SURPASS-CVOT trial, participants were titrated to 15 mg once weekly.
Participants were also titrated to their maximum tolerated dose.
How to Use Mounjaro:
Give once weekly at any time of day, with or without meals.
Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen or thigh.
Another person may inject into the back of the upper arm.
Rotate injection sites with each dose.
Missed dose: Give as soon as possible within 4 days (96 hours).
If more than 4 days have passed, skip the missed dose.
Give the next dose on the regularly scheduled day.
The day of weekly administration can be changed, if necessary.
The time between the 2 doses must be at least 3 days (72 hours).

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
This approval applies to adults with type 2 diabetes.
It applies to those who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist.
It activates two gut hormone receptors.
These receptors help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar.
It works by reducing appetite.
It increases feelings of fullness.
It slows gastric emptying.
It boosts insulin release when blood sugar is high.
It reduces glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe.
It should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes.
It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Do not mix insulin and tirzepatide together in the same injection.
You may give an injection of tirzepatide and insulin in the same body area, but not right next to each other.
Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose.
This dose may be gradually increased.
However, it will not be increased more than once every 4 weeks.
You may change the day of the week you use tirzepatide as long as there are at least three days between doses.
Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor.
Tirzepatide KwikPen:
The KwikPen contains 4 fixed doses.
One dose is injected weekly (subcutaneously).
For your weekly dose, you need to turn the dose knob all the way until it stops.
You also need to ensure the 1 icon is in the dose window.
After 4 doses, throw away (discard) the Pen, including the unused medicine.
The Pen will prevent you from dialing a full dose after you have given yourself 4 weekly doses.
Do not inject the leftover medicine.
Do not transfer the leftover medicine from your Pen into a syringe.

graph_edge.subject: Tirzepatide
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the adverse effect or symptom specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Common Side Effects:
The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
Diarrhea
Vomiting
Constipation
Nausea (mild to moderate)
Decreased appetite
Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:
Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away.
This applies if the pain occurs with or without vomiting.
This also applies if the pain spreads to your back.
Severe stomach pain is a sign of pancreatitis.
Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration.
Dehydration may lead to kidney problems.
Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk.
Tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
Gallbladder problems include severe upper stomach pain.
They include fever.
They include nausea.
They include vomiting.
They include yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice).
They include clay-colored stools.
Serious allergic reactions require seeking emergency medical attention.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug produces its therapeutic effect through the biological mechanism specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
This approval applies to adults with type 2 diabetes.
It applies to those who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist.
It activates two gut hormone receptors.
These receptors help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar.
It works by reducing appetite.
It increases feelings of fullness.
It slows gastric emptying.
It boosts insulin release when blood sugar is high.
It reduces glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe.
It should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes.
It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

- Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
- Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.

Possible Thyroid Tumors (Including Cancer):
Tell your healthcare provider if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath.

candidate_edges.subject: Tirzepatide
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the adverse effect or symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common Side Effects:
The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
Diarrhea
Vomiting
Constipation
Nausea (mild to moderate)
Decreased appetite
Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:
Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away.
This applies if the pain occurs with or without vomiting.
This also applies if the pain spreads to your back.
Severe stomach pain is a sign of pancreatitis.
Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration.
Dehydration may lead to kidney problems.
Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk.
Tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
Gallbladder problems include severe upper stomach pain.
They include fever.
They include nausea.
They include vomiting.
They include yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice).
They include clay-colored stools.
Serious allergic reactions require seeking emergency medical attention.

Methylphenidate may be habit-forming.
Misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death.
Tell your doctor if you have had problems with drug or alcohol abuse.
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect.
Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days.
Examples of such inhibitors include isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.
Methylphenidate may cause new or worsening psychosis.
Psychosis involves unusual thoughts or behavior.
This risk is especially high if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder.
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes.
Call your doctor right away if you have signs of heart problems.
Signs of heart problems include chest pain, feeling light-headed, or being short of breath.
Call your doctor right away if you have signs of psychosis.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
An interaction with methylphenidate could cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome.
Tell your doctor if you or anyone in your family has ever had:
depression, mental illness, bipolar disorder, psychosis, or suicidal thoughts or actions;
blood circulation problems in the hands or feet;
alcoholism or drug addiction; or
if you take Adhansia - an allergy to aspirin or yellow food dye.
phenylketonuria (PKU), as some chewable tablets contain phenylalanine.
To make sure methylphenidate is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have::
problems with the esophagus, stomach, or intestines; or
seizures, epilepsy, or an abnormal brain wave test (EEG).
Becoming dependent on methylphenidate during pregnancy can cause premature birth or low birth weight.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.

The registry is used to track the effects of methylphenidate on the baby.
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using this medicine.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be unsafe or require medical supervision for patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use methylphenidate if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
glaucoma:
pheochromocytoma (tumor of the adrenal gland);
severe high blood pressure or a heart problem;
overactive thyroid;
a personal or family history of tics (muscle twitches) or Tourette's syndrome; or
severe anxiety, tension, or agitation (stimulant medicine can make these symptoms worse).
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in certain people.
Tell your doctor if you have:
heart problems or a congenital heart defect;
high blood pressure; or
a family history of heart disease or sudden death.
Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days.
A dangerous drug interaction could occur.
MAO inhibitors include isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, and tranylcypromine.
Tell your doctor if you also use opioid medicine, herbal products, or medicine for depression, mental illness, Parkinson's disease, migraine headaches, serious infections, or prevention of nausea and vomiting.

An interaction with methylphenidate could cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome.
Tell your doctor if you or anyone in your family has ever had:
depression, mental illness, bipolar disorder, psychosis, or suicidal thoughts or actions;
blood circulation problems in the hands or feet;
alcoholism or drug addiction; or
if you take Adhansia - an allergy to aspirin or yellow food dye.
phenylketonuria (PKU), as some chewable tablets contain phenylalanine.
To make sure methylphenidate is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have::
problems with the esophagus, stomach, or intestines; or
seizures, epilepsy, or an abnormal brain wave test (EEG).
Becoming dependent on methylphenidate during pregnancy can cause premature birth or low birth weight.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry.
The registry is used to track the effects of methylphenidate on the baby.
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using this medicine.

Duloxetine is a selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor antidepressant (SSNRI).
Duloxetine affects chemicals in the brain that may be unbalanced in people with depression.
Duloxetine is used to treat major depressive disorder in adults.
It is also used to treat general anxiety disorder in adults and children who are at least 7 years old.
Duloxetine is also used in adults to treat nerve pain caused by diabetes (diabetic neuropathy).
It is also used to treat chronic muscle or joint pain (such as low back pain and osteoarthritis pain).
Some brands of duloxetine are also used to treat fibromyalgia (a chronic pain disorder).
Drizalma is for treating fibromyalgia only in adults.
Cymbalta may be used to treat fibromyalgia in adults and children at least 13 years old.

How long does it take for prednisone to work?

Some conditions take several days or longer to respond.

:

This means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time.
Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself.
A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands.

What is the difference between prednisone and prednisolone?
:
Prednisone has to be converted by your liver into prednisolone before it can work.
Prednisolone is already in the active form.
For most people the two work in a very similar way at equivalent doses.
Prednisolone is often chosen for people with significant liver disease.
It is also chosen for children.
This is because it comes in liquid forms that are easier to dose.
Does prednisone cause weight gain?
:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone.
It happens for two reasons.
Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water.
Holding onto salt and water adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks.
Prednisone increases appetite.
Increased appetite adds body fat over longer courses.
It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist.
Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop.
Weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.

:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and prednisone.

What is the difference between prednisone and prednisolone?
:
Prednisone has to be converted by your liver into prednisolone before it can work.
Prednisolone is already in the active form.
For most people the two work in a very similar way at equivalent doses.

Does prednisone cause weight gain?
:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone.
It happens for two reasons.
Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water.
Holding onto salt and water adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks.
Prednisone increases appetite.
Increased appetite adds body fat over longer courses.
It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist.
Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop.
Weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.

What is the difference between prednisone and prednisolone?
:
Prednisone has to be converted by your liver into prednisolone before it can work.
Prednisolone is already in the active form.
For most people the two work in a very similar way at equivalent doses.
Prednisolone is often chosen for people with significant liver disease.
It is also chosen for children.

Does prednisone cause weight gain?
:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone.
It happens for two reasons.
Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water.
Holding onto salt and water adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks.
Prednisone increases appetite.
Increased appetite adds body fat over longer courses.
It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist.

Weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.

Is prednisone a steroid?
:
Yes.
Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid.
Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally.
They work by lowering inflammation and immune activity.
They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?
:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour.
Many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day.
Some conditions take several days or longer to respond.
Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them.
Therefore, the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?
:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours.
This means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time.
Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself.
A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands.

Ibuprofen can increase your risk of fatal heart attack, heart failure, or stroke.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking ibuprofen after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to.

This bleeding can be fatal.
These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Do not take more than your recommended dose.
An ibuprofen overdose can damage your stomach or intestines.
Use only the smallest amount of medication needed to get relief from your pain, swelling, or fever.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have any signs of an allergic reaction to buspirone.
Signs of an allergic reaction to buspirone include hives.
Signs of an allergic reaction to buspirone include difficult breathing.
Signs of an allergic reaction to buspirone include swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
chest pain;
shortness of breath; or
a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out.
signs of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Common buspirone side effects may include:
headache;
dizziness, drowsiness;
sleep problems (insomnia);
nausea, upset stomach; or
feeling nervous or excited.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.subject: tramadol

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines.
Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body.
Starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance.
Tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol.
Tell your doctor if you also use:
medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
other opioid medicines
buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine.
These opioids work differently.
They can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms.
So, they are generally not taken with tramadol.
a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax

other opioid medicines

other opioid medicines

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases.
Talk to your doctor if you feel more sensitive to pain.
Talk to your doctor if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Tramadol extended-release capsules and tablets may complicate a healthcare provider’s clinical assessment of an acute abdominal condition.
They are not recommended for people with severe liver or severe kidney impairment.
Taking tramadol during pregnancy may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in the newborn.
These symptoms are known as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS).
Some people are "ultra-rapid metabolizers" of tramadol.
This is because of a variation in an enzyme.
The enzyme is called CYP2D6.
Their bodies convert tramadol into its active form faster than usual.
This can produce dangerously high opioid levels.
This can occur even at a normal dose.
Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason.
This has happened including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids.
Tramadol should not be given to a child younger than 12 years old.

are allergic to tramadol, to any of the other ingredients in your product, or to other opioids

drug or alcohol addiction or
a metabolic disorder.

Head injury or seizures
Problems urinating

candidate_edges.subject: tramadol
candidate_edges.object: opioids generally not taken with tramadol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines.
Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body.
Starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance.
Tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol.
Tell your doctor if you also use:
medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
other opioid medicines
buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine.
These opioids work differently.
They can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms.
So, they are generally not taken with tramadol.
a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax

have significant breathing problems (respiratory depression)

are younger than 12 years of age

drug or alcohol addiction or

Head injury or seizures

Liver, kidney, or thyroid problems

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines.
Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body.
Starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance.
Tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol.
Tell your doctor if you also use:
medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
other opioid medicines
buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine.
These opioids work differently.
They can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms.
So, they are generally not taken with tramadol.
a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Avoid taking supplements or using other products that contain potassium without first asking your doctor.
Salt substitutes or low-salt dietary products often contain potassium.
If you take certain products together you may accidentally get too much potassium.
Read the label of any other medicine you are using to see if it contains potassium.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.object: not a complete list of side effects
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include hives.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include difficult breathing.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
severe throat irritation;
stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
gas, stomach pain; or
the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not miss any scheduled appointments.

Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor.
If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on an extended-release tablet or capsule.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take potassium chloride exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Take potassium chloride with a full glass of water.
Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
Measure liquid medicine with the dosing syringe provided, or with a special dose-measuring spoon or medicine cup.
If you do not have a dose-measuring device, ask your pharmacist for one.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on a tablet or capsule.
Sucking on the pill could irritate your mouth or throat.
Call your doctor if you have trouble swallowing a potassium chloride capsule or tablet.
You may be able to dissolve the tablet in water.
You may be able to mix the medicine from a capsule with soft food.
Carefully follow your doctor's instructions.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.object: call your doctor for medical advice about side effects
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include hives.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include difficult breathing.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
severe throat irritation;
stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
gas, stomach pain; or
the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.object: do not stop taking without talking to doctor
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia).
You should not use potassium chloride if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition.
Your blood may need to be tested often.
Your heart rate may also be checked.
The heart rate can be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG.
An electrocardiograph or ECG is sometimes called an EKG.
The device is used to measure electrical activity of the heart.
This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium.
Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat.
They include muscle weakness or limp feeling.
They include severe stomach pain.
They include numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor.
If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on an extended-release tablet or capsule.

The dose depends on what you are being treated for.
The same doses apply to hydroxyzine hydrochloride tablets.
The same doses apply to hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution.
The same doses apply to hydroxyzine pamoate capsules.
Dosage for anxiety and tension:
Adults: 50 to 100 mg four times a day
Children under 6 years: 50 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Children 6 years and over: 50 to 100 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Dosage for itching:
Adults: 25 mg three or four times a day
Children under 6 years: 50 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Children 6 years and over: 50 to 100 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Dosage for sedation before and after surgery:
Adults: 50 to 100 mg
Children: 0.6 mg for each kilogram of body weight
Treatment can be started with an injection into a muscle.
Later doses can be given by mouth.
Dosage in older adults:
Doctors usually start older adults on a low dose.
Sedating medicines can cause confusion and too much sedation in older people.
Your doctor will watch you closely.
Kidney, liver, and heart function often decline with age.

graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is available in the pharmaceutical dosage form specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) and hydroxyzine pamoate are two salt forms of the same active medicine.
Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses.
It gives them the same doses.
It gives them the same warnings.
It gives them the same side effects.
The injection is the exception.
It is a hydroxyzine HCl product.
There is no pamoate injection.
It has its own approved uses, doses, and warnings.
The practical differences are:
Form.
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride comes as tablets and as an oral solution.
Hydroxyzine pamoate comes as capsules.
How they dissolve.
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride is very soluble in water.
Hydroxyzine pamoate is practically insoluble in water.
How the strength is measured.
Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by the amount of hydroxyzine HCl they are equivalent to.
A 25 mg pamoate capsule delivers the same amount of active medicine as a hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg tablet.
The two salts also had different brand names.
Vistaril was the brand name for hydroxyzine pamoate.
Atarax was the brand name for hydroxyzine hydrochloride.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine is a prescription antihistamine.
It is used to treat anxiety and tension.
It is used to treat itching from allergic skin conditions.
It is used for sedation before and after general anesthesia.
It comes in three oral forms:
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) tablets in 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg strengths
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution (a syrup) containing 10 mg in each 5 mL
Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules in 25 mg
There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection.
It is given into a muscle by a healthcare professional and is never given into a vein or under the skin.
Hydroxyzine is not chemically related to benzodiazepines, phenothiazines, reserpine, or meprobamate.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine hydrochloride
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is available in the pharmaceutical dosage form specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) and hydroxyzine pamoate are two salt forms of the same active medicine.
Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses.
It gives them the same doses.
It gives them the same warnings.
It gives them the same side effects.
The injection is the exception.
It is a hydroxyzine HCl product.
There is no pamoate injection.
It has its own approved uses, doses, and warnings.
The practical differences are:
Form.
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride comes as tablets and as an oral solution.
Hydroxyzine pamoate comes as capsules.
How they dissolve.
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride is very soluble in water.
Hydroxyzine pamoate is practically insoluble in water.
How the strength is measured.
Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by the amount of hydroxyzine HCl they are equivalent to.
A 25 mg pamoate capsule delivers the same amount of active medicine as a hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg tablet.
The two salts also had different brand names.
Vistaril was the brand name for hydroxyzine pamoate.
Atarax was the brand name for hydroxyzine hydrochloride.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is given through the route of administration specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses.
These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
Anxiety and tension.
For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
Itching from allergic skin conditions.
For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant.
It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
Sedation around surgery.
As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting.
It is usually given in hospital or clinic settings.
It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety.
Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months.
Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain.
These regions are located below the outer layer known as the cortex.
It is not a cortical depressant.
It does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain.
Some other sedatives work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction.
This is what relieves itching.
Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle.
Hydroxyzine widens the airways (bronchodilation).
Hydroxyzine reduces pain.
These are effects that have been observed rather than uses the medicine is approved for.
Hydroxyzine has also been shown to reduce nausea and vomiting.
This is an approved use for the injection.
It is not an approved use for the forms taken by mouth.

graph_edge.subject: Hydroxyzine
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug produces its therapeutic effect through the biological mechanism specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain.
These regions are located below the outer layer known as the cortex.
It is not a cortical depressant.
It does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain.
Some other sedatives work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction.
This is what relieves itching.
Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle.
Hydroxyzine widens the airways (bronchodilation).

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine makes the effects of central nervous system depressants stronger.
If you take hydroxyzine with any of the following, your doctor may need to lower the dose of the other medicine.
narcotic (opioid) pain medicines
non-narcotic pain medicines
barbiturates
Hydroxyzine may increase the effects of meperidine and barbiturates when used before anesthesia.
Your doctor will adjust these doses for you individually.
Care is needed if you take other medicines.
These medicines can affect heart rhythm.
They do this by prolonging the QT interval.
These include:
heart rhythm medicines such as quinidine, procainamide, amiodarone, and sotalol
certain antipsychotics such as ziprasidone, iloperidone, clozapine, quetiapine, and chlorpromazine
certain antidepressants such as citalopram and fluoxetine
certain antibiotics such as azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin, gatifloxacin, and moxifloxacin
other medicines such as pentamidine, methadone, ondansetron, and droperidol
Hydroxyzine does not affect atropine or other belladonna alkaloids.
It is not known to interfere with digitalis.

allergic reaction

Anxiety and tension.

Itching from allergic skin conditions.

The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting.
It is usually given in hospital or clinic settings.
It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety.
Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months.
Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses.

Form.
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride comes as tablets and as an oral solution.
Hydroxyzine pamoate comes as capsules.

How the strength is measured.

Vistaril was the brand name for hydroxyzine pamoate.
Atarax was the brand name for hydroxyzine hydrochloride.

narcotic (opioid) pain medicines
non-narcotic pain medicines
barbiturates

certain antipsychotics such as ziprasidone, iloperidone, clozapine, quetiapine, and chlorpromazine
certain antidepressants such as citalopram and fluoxetine
certain antibiotics such as azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin, gatifloxacin, and moxifloxacin
other medicines such as pentamidine, methadone, ondansetron, and droperidol
Hydroxyzine does not affect atropine or other belladonna alkaloids.
It is not known to interfere with digitalis.

Anxiety and tension.

Itching from allergic skin conditions.
For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant.
It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
Sedation around surgery.
As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting.
It is usually given in hospital or clinic settings.
It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety.

The dose depends on what you are being treated for.
The same doses apply to hydroxyzine hydrochloride tablets.
The same doses apply to hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution.
The same doses apply to hydroxyzine pamoate capsules.
Dosage for anxiety and tension:
Adults: 50 to 100 mg four times a day
Children under 6 years: 50 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Children 6 years and over: 50 to 100 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Dosage for itching:
Adults: 25 mg three or four times a day
Children under 6 years: 50 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Children 6 years and over: 50 to 100 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Dosage for sedation before and after surgery:
Adults: 50 to 100 mg
Children: 0.6 mg for each kilogram of body weight
Treatment can be started with an injection into a muscle.
Later doses can be given by mouth.
Dosage in older adults:
Doctors usually start older adults on a low dose.
Sedating medicines can cause confusion and too much sedation in older people.
Your doctor will watch you closely.
Kidney, liver, and heart function often decline with age.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may require changes in dosage based on the condition or factor specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine makes the effects of central nervous system depressants stronger.
If you take hydroxyzine with any of the following, your doctor may need to lower the dose of the other medicine.
narcotic (opioid) pain medicines
non-narcotic pain medicines
barbiturates
Hydroxyzine may increase the effects of meperidine and barbiturates when used before anesthesia.
Your doctor will adjust these doses for you individually.
Care is needed if you take other medicines.
These medicines can affect heart rhythm.
They do this by prolonging the QT interval.
These include:
heart rhythm medicines such as quinidine, procainamide, amiodarone, and sotalol
certain antipsychotics such as ziprasidone, iloperidone, clozapine, quetiapine, and chlorpromazine
certain antidepressants such as citalopram and fluoxetine
certain antibiotics such as azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin, gatifloxacin, and moxifloxacin
other medicines such as pentamidine, methadone, ondansetron, and droperidol
Hydroxyzine does not affect atropine or other belladonna alkaloids.
It is not known to interfere with digitalis.

Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors.
It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body.
High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout.
Gout is a type of arthritis.
In gout, uric acid builds up in the joints.
Uric acid is a naturally occurring substance in the body.
The buildup of uric acid causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat.
These attacks occur in one or more joints.
Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur.
Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid.
The high levels of uric acid build up in the blood.
This buildup occurs as tumors break down.
This happens in people with certain types of cancer.
These people are being treated with chemotherapy medications.
It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back.
This occurs in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

Allopurinol can lower blood cells that help your body fight infections.
This can make it easier for you to bleed from an injury or get sick from being around others who are ill.
Your blood may need to be tested often.
Visit your doctor regularly.
In rare cases, allopurinol may cause a severe allergic reaction.
Stop taking this medicine.
Call your doctor right away if you have painful urination.
Call your doctor right away if you have blood in your urine.
Call your doctor right away if you have burning in your eyes.
Call your doctor right away if you have swelling in your face or throat.
Call your doctor right away if you have skin redness.
Call your doctor right away if you have a rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling.
Avoid drinking alcohol.

Allopurinol may impair your thinking or reactions.
Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

candidate_edges.subject: Allopurinol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the serious or potentially dangerous adverse effect specified by the object entity that requires medical attention.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to allopurinol.
Signs of an allergic reaction to allopurinol include hives, difficult breathing, and swelling in your face or throat.
Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction.
Signs of a severe skin reaction include fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, and a red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling.
Seek medical treatment if you have a serious drug reaction that can affect many parts of your body.
Symptoms may include skin rash, fever, swollen glands, muscle aches, severe weakness, unusual bruising, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.
Allopurinol may cause serious side effects.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
any skin rash, no matter how mild;
painful urination, blood in the urine;
inflammation of your blood vessels - numbness or tingling, skin rash, fever, headache, body aches, night sweats, weight loss, feeling or weak or tired;

candidate_edges.subject: Allopurinol
candidate_edges.object: drink 8 to 10 full glasses of fluid every day to reduce risk of kidney stones
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take allopurinol exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take the tablets with a full glass of water.
To reduce your risk of kidney stones, drink 8 to 10 full glasses of fluid every day.
Do this unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
Take allopurinol tablets after meals to help prevent stomach upset.
Allopurinol injection is injected into a vein by a healthcare provider.
The injection is usually only used if you are unable to take medicine by mouth.
You may need frequent medical tests while using this medicine.
You may need these tests even if you have no symptoms.
Your kidney and liver function may also need to be tested.
Your doctor may change your dose if your kidney function changes.
You may have gout attacks when you first start taking allopurinol tablets.
Your doctor may recommend another gout medication to take with allopurinol.
Keep taking the medicine as directed.
Your symptoms may not improve for up to 2 to 6 weeks.

candidate_edges.subject: Allopurinol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: Patients taking the subject drug may need the medical test or monitoring specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take allopurinol exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take the tablets with a full glass of water.
To reduce your risk of kidney stones, drink 8 to 10 full glasses of fluid every day.
Do this unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
Take allopurinol tablets after meals to help prevent stomach upset.
Allopurinol injection is injected into a vein by a healthcare provider.
The injection is usually only used if you are unable to take medicine by mouth.
You may need frequent medical tests while using this medicine.
You may need these tests even if you have no symptoms.
Your kidney and liver function may also need to be tested.
Your doctor may change your dose if your kidney function changes.
You may have gout attacks when you first start taking allopurinol tablets.
Your doctor may recommend another gout medication to take with allopurinol.
Keep taking the medicine as directed.
Your symptoms may not improve for up to 2 to 6 weeks.

Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors.
It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body.
High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout.
Gout is a type of arthritis.
In gout, uric acid builds up in the joints.
Uric acid is a naturally occurring substance in the body.
The buildup of uric acid causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat.
These attacks occur in one or more joints.
Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur.
Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid.
The high levels of uric acid build up in the blood.
This buildup occurs as tumors break down.
This happens in people with certain types of cancer.
These people are being treated with chemotherapy medications.
It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back.
This occurs in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to prevent or lower the risk of the medical event or condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors.
It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body.
High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout.
Gout is a type of arthritis.
In gout, uric acid builds up in the joints.
Uric acid is a naturally occurring substance in the body.
The buildup of uric acid causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat.
These attacks occur in one or more joints.
Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur.
Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid.
The high levels of uric acid build up in the blood.
This buildup occurs as tumors break down.
This happens in people with certain types of cancer.
These people are being treated with chemotherapy medications.
It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back.
This occurs in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

candidate_edges.subject: Allopurinol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: Patients taking the subject drug may need the medical test or monitoring specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use this medicine if you have ever had an allergic reaction to allopurinol.
Allopurinol can lower blood cells that help your body fight infections.
This can make it easier for you to bleed from an injury or get sick from being around others who are ill.
Your blood may need to be tested often.
Visit your doctor regularly.
In rare cases, allopurinol may cause a severe allergic reaction.
Stop taking this medicine.
Call your doctor right away if you have painful urination.
Call your doctor right away if you have blood in your urine.
Call your doctor right away if you have burning in your eyes.
Call your doctor right away if you have swelling in your face or throat.
Call your doctor right away if you have skin redness.
Call your doctor right away if you have a rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling.
Avoid drinking alcohol.
It can make your condition worse.
Allopurinol may impair your thinking or reactions.
Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take allopurinol exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take the tablets with a full glass of water.
To reduce your risk of kidney stones, drink 8 to 10 full glasses of fluid every day.
Do this unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
Take allopurinol tablets after meals to help prevent stomach upset.
Allopurinol injection is injected into a vein by a healthcare provider.
The injection is usually only used if you are unable to take medicine by mouth.
You may need frequent medical tests while using this medicine.
You may need these tests even if you have no symptoms.
Your kidney and liver function may also need to be tested.
Your doctor may change your dose if your kidney function changes.
You may have gout attacks when you first start taking allopurinol tablets.
Your doctor may recommend another gout medication to take with allopurinol.
Keep taking the medicine as directed.
Your symptoms may not improve for up to 2 to 6 weeks.

graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug carries the warning specified by the object entity regarding use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
You should not use clopidogrel if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
any active bleeding; or
a stomach ulcer or bleeding in the brain (such as from a head injury).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
an ulcer in your stomach or intestines; or
a bleeding disorder or blood clotting disorder.
Clopidogrel may not work as well.
This may happen if you have certain genetic factors.
These genetic factors affect the breakdown of this medicine in your body.
Your doctor may perform a blood test to make sure clopidogrel is right for you.
This medicine is not expected to harm an unborn baby.
However, taking clopidogrel within 1 week before childbirth can cause bleeding in the mother.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
You should not breastfeed while using this medicine.

candidate_edges.subject: clopidogrel
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the serious or potentially dangerous adverse effect specified by the object entity that requires medical attention.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use clopidogrel if you have any active bleeding such as a stomach ulcer or bleeding in the brain.
Clopidogrel increases your risk of bleeding, which can be severe or life-threatening.
Call your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have bleeding that will not stop.
Call your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have blood in your urine.
Call your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have black or bloody stools.
Call your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you cough up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Do not stop taking clopidogrel without first talking to your doctor, even if you have signs of bleeding.
Stopping clopidogrel may increase your risk of a heart attack or stroke.

candidate_edges.subject: clopidogrel
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be unsafe or require medical supervision for patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use clopidogrel if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
any active bleeding; or
a stomach ulcer or bleeding in the brain (such as from a head injury).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
an ulcer in your stomach or intestines; or
a bleeding disorder or blood clotting disorder.
Clopidogrel may not work as well.
This may happen if you have certain genetic factors.
These genetic factors affect the breakdown of this medicine in your body.
Your doctor may perform a blood test to make sure clopidogrel is right for you.
This medicine is not expected to harm an unborn baby.
However, taking clopidogrel within 1 week before childbirth can cause bleeding in the mother.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
You should not breastfeed while using this medicine.

candidate_edges.subject: clopidogrel
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is typically prescribed at the dose or dosing regimen specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Usual Adult Dose for Acute Coronary Syndrome:
Unstable Angina (UA)/Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) has a loading dose of 300 mg orally once.
The maintenance dose is 75 mg orally once a day.
The duration of therapy is optimal unknown.
ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) has an optional loading dose of 300 mg orally once.
The maintenance dose is 75 mg orally once a day, with or without thrombolytics.
The optimal duration of therapy is unknown.
Comments: -Administer this drug in combination with aspirin 75 mg to 325 mg orally once a day.
The benefit of this drug is unknown.
This applies to patients who undergo primary percutaneous coronary intervention.
Uses include prevention of atherothrombotic events.
This applies to patients with non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome.
This includes patients with UA.
This includes patients with NSTEMI.
This includes those who are to be managed medically.
This includes those who are to be managed with coronary revascularization.
This also applies to patients with STEMI.
Usual Adult Dose for Ischemic Stroke:

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used together with the other treatment or lifestyle measure specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Use these medicines exactly as directed.
Clopidogrel can be taken with or without food.
Clopidogrel is sometimes taken together with aspirin.
Take aspirin only if your doctor tells you to.
Clopidogrel keeps your blood from coagulating (clotting).

Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.

graph_edge.subject: Ergocalciferol
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject entity is identified as or is equivalent to the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Ergocalciferol is vitamin D2.
Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium.
Ergocalciferol is used to treat hypoparathyroidism (decreased functioning of the parathyroid glands).
Ergocalciferol is also used to treat rickets.
Rickets is the softening of the bones caused by vitamin D deficiency.
Ergocalciferol is also used to treat low levels of phosphate in the blood.
Low levels of phosphate in the blood are known as hypophosphatemia.
Ergocalciferol may also be used for purposes not listed in this medication guide.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
heart disease;
kidney disease; or
an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about.
These ingredients include peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes.
Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby.
Your dose needs may be different during pregnancy.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk.
It may cause side effects in the nursing baby.
Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice.

candidate_edges.subject: Ergocalciferol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be unsafe or require medical supervision for patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
heart disease;
kidney disease; or
an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about.
These ingredients include peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes.
Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby.
Your dose needs may be different during pregnancy.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk.
It may cause side effects in the nursing baby.
Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice.

candidate_edges.subject: Ergocalciferol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be unsafe or require medical supervision for patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
heart disease;
kidney disease; or
an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about.
These ingredients include peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes.
Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby.
Your dose needs may be different during pregnancy.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk.
It may cause side effects in the nursing baby.
Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice.

Usual Adult Dose of Ondansetron for Nausea/Vomiting -- Chemotherapy Induced:
Oral administration is recommended for Highly Emetogenic Cancer Chemotherapy (HEC).
The recommended oral dose for HEC is 24 mg.
This dose should be taken 30 minutes before the start of single-day HEC.
This recommendation includes cisplatin doses of 50 mg/m2 or greater.
Oral administration is recommended for Moderately Emetogenic Cancer Chemotherapy (MEC).
The recommended oral dose for MEC is 8 mg.
The first dose of 8 mg should be taken twice a day.
The first dose is administered 30 minutes before the start of chemotherapy.
The subsequent dose is administered 8 hours later.
After the initial doses, 8 mg is taken orally 2 times a day.
These subsequent doses are given every 12 hours.
This regimen continues for 1 to 2 days after the completion of chemotherapy.
Parenteral administration is recommended.
The recommended parenteral dose is 0.15 mg/kg IV.
The first dose is infused over 15 minutes.
The first dose is given 30 minutes before the start of emetogenic chemotherapy.

reference_evidence:

graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the serious or potentially dangerous adverse effect specified by the object entity that requires medical attention.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Ondansetron can cause a serious heart problem.
This risk is especially high if you use certain medicines at the same time.
These medicines include antibiotics, antidepressants, heart rhythm medicine, antipsychotic medicines, and medicines to treat cancer, malaria, HIV or AIDS.
Tell your doctor about all medicines you use, and those you start or stop using during your treatment with ondansetron.
Taking ondansetron while using certain other medicines can cause high levels of serotonin to build up in your body.
This condition is called "serotonin syndrome."
Serotonin syndrome can be fatal.
Tell your doctor if you also use:
medicine to treat depression;
medicine to treat a psychiatric disorder;
a narcotic (opioid) medication; or
medicine to prevent nausea and vomiting.
This list is not complete and many other drugs can interact with ondansetron.
This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you.

This combination helps relieve pain, tenderness, and limited movement.

Cyclobenzaprine is used to treat fibromyalgia in adults.
It can help reduce pain.
For fibromyalgia, it is taken as a sublingual (under the tongue) tablet at bedtime under the brand name Tonmya.
In clinical trials, Tonmya significantly reduced fibromyalgia pain compared with placebo over 14 weeks.
Close to half of treated patients achieved at least a 30% improvement in pain.

These signals drive muscle tone and spasm.
